content: The discussion on 3-NRTI regimens has been removed from this section because these regimens are no longer recommended for antiretroviral therapy (ART)-naïve patients. The recommendation for initiating ART in patients with early HIV infection has been updated from should be considered optional (CIII) to should be offered (BII). The guidance on the use of efavirenz (EFV) during pregnancy has been revised to align with the Perinatal Antiretroviral Guidelines. Specifically, the updated recommendation states: Because the risk of neural tube defects is limited to the first 5 to 6 weeks of pregnancy, and pregnancy is rarely recognized before 4 to 6 weeks of gestation, EFV can be continued in pregnant women receiving an EFV-based regimen who present for antenatal care in the first trimester, provided the regimen produces virologic suppression (CIII). The Panel also recommends that intravenous zidovudine during labor may be omitted in women with HIV RNA levels <400 copies/mL near delivery (BII). A new section titled Pharmacokinetic (PK) Enhancing has been added, which describes the roles and mechanisms of ritonavir (RTV) and cobicistat (COBI) as pharmacokinetic enhancers to increase the exposure of antiretroviral drugs. Minor revisions have been made to the following sections: Introduction, Adverse Effects of Antiretroviral Agents, and ART for the treatment of HIV infection. Since the advent of potent combination therapy in 1996, ART has steadily improved. New drugs with novel mechanisms of action, enhanced potency, activity against multidrug-resistant viruses, improved dosing convenience, and better tolerability have been approved. ART has significantly reduced HIV-associated morbidity and mortality, transforming HIV into a chronic, manageable condition. Furthermore, effective ART in HIV-infected individuals is highly effective in preventing transmission to sexual partners. However, less than one-third of HIV-infected individuals in the United States have suppressed viral loads, primarily due to undiagnosed HIV infection and failure to link or retain diagnosed patients in care. Despite remarkable progress in HIV treatment and prevention, economic and social barriers continue to contribute to morbidity, mortality, and new HIV infections. The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Panel on Antiretroviral Guidelines for Adults and Adolescents, a working group of the Office of AIDS Research Advisory Council (OARAC), aims to provide HIV care practitioners with recommendations based on current knowledge of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for treating adults and adolescents with HIV in the United States. The Panel reviews new evidence and updates recommendations as needed. The Panel's focus areas include baseline assessment, treatment goals, indications for ART initiation, selection of initial regimens for ART-naïve patients, drugs or combinations to avoid, management of adverse effects and drug interactions, management of treatment failure, and special ART-related considerations in specific patient populations. For recommendations on pre-exposure HIV prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV-uninfected individuals, refer to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidelines. These guidelines represent the current state of knowledge regarding ARV use. However, as HIV science evolves rapidly, new agents and clinical data may change therapeutic options and preferences. Information in these guidelines may not always align with FDA-approved labeling for specific products or indications. Clinicians should exercise clinical judgment tailored to individual patient circumstances. The Panel emphasizes the importance of clinical research to address unanswered questions about the optimal safety and efficacy of ART. It encourages the development of protocols and patient participation in well-designed, IRB-approved clinical trials. Recommendations in these guidelines are based on scientific evidence and expert opinion. Each recommendation includes a letter (A, B, or C) indicating the strength of the recommendation and a Roman numeral (I, II, or III) representing the quality of evidence supporting the recommendation. Studies have shown that outcomes in HIV-infected outpatients are better when care is delivered by clinicians with HIV expertise, reflecting the complexity of HIV infection and its treatment. Appropriate training, experience, and ongoing education are essential for optimal care. Primary care providers without HIV expertise, especially in rural or underserved areas, should identify regional experts for consultation when needed. Every HIV-infected patient entering care should undergo a comprehensive medical history, physical examination, laboratory evaluation, and counseling on the implications of HIV infection. The goals of the initial evaluation are to confirm the HIV diagnosis, obtain baseline historical and laboratory data, ensure patient understanding of HIV infection and transmission, and initiate care as recommended in HIV primary care and opportunistic infection guidelines. Baseline laboratory tests should include HIV antibody testing (if prior documentation is unavailable), CD4 T-cell count, plasma HIV RNA (viral load), complete blood count, chemistry profile, transaminase levels, BUN, creatinine, urinalysis, hepatitis serologies, fasting blood glucose, serum lipids, and genotypic resistance testing. CD4 T-cell count is a critical indicator of immune function in HIV-infected patients. It determines the urgency of ART initiation, the need for opportunistic infection prophylaxis, and predicts disease progression and survival. ART is now recommended for all HIV-infected patients. CD4 counts should be monitored every 3 to 6 months in untreated patients and less frequently in those with stable clinical and immunologic status on ART. Plasma HIV-1 RNA (viral load) is the most important indicator of response to ART. Viral load testing should be performed at baseline and regularly thereafter, especially in patients on treatment. Optimal viral suppression is defined as a viral load persistently below the level of detection (<200 copies/mL). Drug-resistance testing is recommended for all HIV-infected individuals at entry into care, regardless of whether ART will be initiated immediately. Genotypic resistance testing is preferred for guiding therapy in ART-naïve patients and those with virologic failure. Phenotypic assays may be added for patients with complex resistance patterns. Resistance testing should be performed while the patient is on prescribed ARV drugs or within four weeks of discontinuation. Clinicians are encouraged to consult HIV drug resistance specialists to interpret test results and design optimal regimens.
